newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Papua mercenary contract cancelled - pilots.
newsitem.headline: Papua mercenary contract cancelled - pilots.

text.p: Papua New Guinea has cancelled a controversial contract for the hire of mercenaries to help its battle with rebels on Bougainville island, a departing helicopter pilot said on Wednesday.
"The contract's terminated. It's as simple as that. It's better for both sides," the pilot told reporters in Singapore.

The contract had been with British-based Sandline International, which has used South Africa-based Executive Outcomes to supply the mercenaries. Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan told a news conference in Port Moresby earlier on Wednesday, in an apparent olive branch to the rebels, that he was considering cancelling the contract.
Chan has been criticised internationally over the plan to bring in mercenaries to help battle the rebels on resource-rich Bougainville island, 900 km (560 miles) northeast of the capital.
"The cancellation of Sandline, as demanded by the petition, will be considered by the cabinet," Chan said. "But we must not be too premature about making that decision."
But two pilots, who declined to be identified, told reporters while in transit on their way home to South Africa, that the contract was over.
"The contract was stopped by mutual agreement," said one.
The pilots said they had only arrived in Papua New Guinea on Sunday. They were among a group of six Sandline men who left the impoverished nation on Wednesday.
They said their remaining 34 colleagues would leave once logistical problems, which they did not specify, were sorted out. The 34 have been confined to barracks in the north.
The pilots at first described themselves as civil aviation advisers after arriving in Singapore before admitting they were Sandline helicopter pilots.
Their four colleagues declined to talk to reporters.
"On Sunday we were stalled. We were supposed to fly and the aircraft was supposed to be in on Tuesday," said one.
But earlier on Wednesday, a major in the Papua New Guinea defence forces told them they had to leave.
The pilots said they had no regrets in having gone.
When asked whether their presence had helped, one said: "Yes, I think it has."
"It was a wake-up call. There were nine years of Bougainville and it should have been stopped a long time ago -- whatever, political, military wise, anything," he said.
Protesters on Wednesday delivered a petition which called for the mercenaries to be sent home and for Chan to resign.

Chan told Wednesday's news conference he was in complete control of the South Pacific nation, which was thrown into chaos when he sacked its army chief who had demanded Chan's resignation over the mercenary plans.
